justice: The street space is dominated by a single undivided carriageway, while no dedicated sidewalk is visible on either side, so pedestrian space is not equitably allocated.
Road edges transition directly into dirt shoulders, parked cars, and informal structures, which suggests uneven access conditions for different users along the corridor.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or barrier-free pedestrian facilities are visible, limiting accessibility for users with mobility, vision, or stroller needs.
The narrow paved lane appears usable by cars, walkers, and cyclists together, but the lack of formal separation means weaker fairness in protecting slower and more vulnerable users.
safety: There are no visible lane markings, sidewalks, bike lanes, or traffic-calming devices, increasing conflict risk among mixed users on the same narrow roadway.
Several cars are parked partly on the roadside dirt area close to the travel lane, which may create visibility and maneuvering conflicts.
Utility poles and overhead wires line the street, but no streetlights are clearly visible, which may reduce perceived safety after dark.
The road appears relatively low-speed and low-traffic at the moment, which slightly improves safety despite the lack of formal protective infrastructure.
livability: The street has residential buildings and small roadside structures, indicating basic daily living activity and local occupancy.
However, there are no visible public amenities such as benches, bus stops, playgrounds, or community gathering spaces to support broader street life.
Unpaved shoulders, exposed soil, and scattered roadside materials reduce the sense of a well-served and socially supportive public environment.
The presence of laundry hanging outside and small structures suggests lived-in neighborhood activity, but the public realm remains weakly equipped.
sustainability: A few street trees are present on the right side, providing limited ecological value and some shade.
The street lacks visible green infrastructure such as planting strips, rain gardens, or permeable sidewalk systems along most of its length.
No dedicated public transport stop, cycling facility, or other clear low-carbon mobility infrastructure is visible in the scene.
Large areas of bare soil and minimally landscaped edges suggest low environmental performance and limited stormwater management.
aesthetics: The large tree on the right adds a natural focal point and softens the otherwise hard linear street view.
The streetscape shows mixed building quality, with newer houses in the distance but also improvised sheds and weathered facades in the foreground, reducing visual coherence.
Overhead utility wires, exposed dirt shoulders, and scattered roadside materials create visual clutter.
The street appears relatively open and clean in the travel lane itself, which prevents the aesthetic quality from being extremely low.
comfort: Thermal comfort is limited because shade is sparse overall; apart from one major tree on the right, most of the roadway is exposed to sun.
Physical comfort is weakened by the absence of a formal sidewalk, leaving pedestrians to walk either on the concrete roadway or uneven dirt edges.
No benches, shelters, or resting facilities are visible, reducing comfort for longer stays or slower-moving users.
Psychological comfort is mixed: the street looks quiet and not crowded, but informal edges, parked vehicles, and weak separation between users may create uncertainty.
walkability: There is no continuous sidewalk visible, so walking routes are not clearly protected from motor traffic.
The road surface itself is relatively even and paved, which supports basic walking movement, but pedestrians would need to share space with vehicles.
No marked crossings, curb extensions, pedestrian signs, or route guidance elements are visible.
Dirt shoulders and informal roadside obstructions near buildings reduce continuity and ease for side-by-side walking.
bikeability: The street appears low-speed and low-volume, which can make basic cycling possible in mixed traffic.
However, there are no bike lanes, edge markings, or cycling-specific protections anywhere in the visible corridor.
Parked cars along the roadside can introduce opening-door and merging conflicts for cyclists.
The lack of dedicated bicycle parking, signage, and intersection treatments limits overall cycling convenience and safety.
